lesson.title: The Attraction Hiding in Every Molecule
lesson.summary: London dispersion forces are weak, temporary attractions that arise from momentary, shifting imbalances in electron distribution, and they are present to some degree in every atom and molecule, polar or nonpolar.
lesson.body:
Among the intermolecular forces introduced earlier, London dispersion forces are the most universal, because unlike dipole-dipole forces, they do not require a molecule to have any permanent charge separation at all. They arise instead from the constant, random motion of electrons. At any given instant, the electrons surrounding an atom or molecule are not perfectly evenly distributed; by pure chance, a bit more electron density might momentarily sit on one side than the other, creating a fleeting, temporary dipole where none existed a moment before. That instantaneous dipole then distorts the electron cloud of a neighboring atom or molecule, pushing its electrons away and inducing a matching temporary dipole in the neighbor, aligned so that the two attract each other. This is why the forces are sometimes described as induced dipole, induced dipole attractions.

Because this effect depends only on having electrons that can shift around, London dispersion forces exist between every pair of atoms or molecules, including the noble gases, which have no bonds at all to be polar or nonpolar, and including perfectly nonpolar molecules like N2 or CO2. This universality is exactly why nonpolar substances can still be condensed into liquids or solids at low enough temperature. Helium, the least polarizable and lowest mass noble gas, has such weak dispersion forces that it remains a gas down to about negative 269 degrees Celsius, only 4 degrees above absolute zero, and even then only liquefies under specific conditions rather than freezing at ordinary pressure. This extreme case illustrates just how weak dispersion forces are compared with any bond, while still confirming that some attraction, however faint, is present.

The strength of London dispersion forces increases with the number of electrons in a molecule, because more electrons mean a larger, more easily distorted electron cloud capable of forming bigger temporary dipoles, a property called polarizability that is explored in full in the next section. This produces a clean and testable trend within the halogens: F2, with few electrons, is a gas at room temperature; Cl2, with more electrons, is also a gas but liquefies at a higher temperature than F2; Br2, with even more electrons, is a liquid at room temperature; and I2, with the most electrons of the four, is a solid at room temperature. Since these four molecules are all nonpolar and have essentially the same shape, this steady increase in boiling and melting point across the group is attributable almost entirely to the increasing strength of London dispersion forces as electron count rises.

Because dispersion forces grow with molecular size and electron count, they are not confined to nonpolar molecules; they act between polar molecules too, layered underneath any dipole-dipole attraction those molecules also experience, exactly as previewed when intermolecular forces were introduced. In sufficiently large molecules, dispersion forces can even become the dominant intermolecular attraction, outweighing a modest permanent dipole, which is why some larger polar molecules can have lower boiling points than smaller nonpolar molecules with many more electrons. London dispersion forces, though often the weakest force acting in any single comparison, are therefore never negligible and are frequently the deciding factor in the overall strength ranking of intermolecular attraction.
